newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda says U.N. genocide tribunal useless.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says U.N. genocide tribunal useless.

text.p: Rwanda on Sunday condemned the United Nations tribunal set up to try those suspected of taking part in the 1994 genocide as a crippled body that required major changes.
Rwanda's reaction came 11 days after a top-level report from the U.N. itself criticised the court.
A government statement in Kigali attacked the international tribunal, based at Arusha in Tanzania, for a long list of supposed failures.
It alleged poor organisation, failure to investigate crimes, failure to bring suspects to trial and failure to work with the Rwandan government.
The report also attacked Canadian prosecutor Louise Arbour and questioned her abilities.
"She is simply not equipped to handle the trials -- leave alone heading the tribunal," the statement said.
The tribunal was set up at the end of 1994, months after gruesome images of the slaughter of 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in a wave of genocide shocked the world.
But so far only one person has been brought to trial and only a handful are indicted, awaiting trial.
A U.N. report earlier this month accused the Arusha tribunal of inefficiency and waste, mismanagement and corruption.
Rwanda has in the past condemned the tribunal for its slow pace and its inability to bring those most seriously implicated in the genocide to trial.
The tribunal can deliver only prison sentences, while Rwanda wants death for the most serious offenders.
In Rwanda itself, at least 11 death sentences have been handed out by genocide courts which began sitting in December.
Another 90,000 people are awaiting trial in overcrowded prisons, accused of varying levels of participation in the genocide.
But the biggest ringleaders, in exile, have so far escaped both the Rwandan government and the United Nations.

Rwanda recommended that the U.N. tribunal prosecutor should have more powers. It also said the tribunal should have its own prosecutor for Rwandan war crimes instead of sharing one with the tribunal for former Yugoslavia.
The statement also called for clearly set out strategy and for staff with more experience of criminal investigations and sensitivity to local customs.
"They have exhumed mass graves without notice to the authorities or the relatives of the dead and left the remains on site, an abomination in our culture," it said.
It called for the tribunal, or at least the prosecutor's office, to be transferred from Arusha to Kigali and for the tribunal to improve its relations with the government.
"Personnel of the tribunal...have behaved with hostility, arrogance and insensitivity that is difficult to explain," the statement said.
